components.gap: (1) Durrett (p. 214, PDF p. 222) states that regular conditional distributions do not always exist, attributes the first example to Dieudonne (1948), refers to Doob (1953) p. 624 and Faden (1985), and explains the source of the failure: for each countable disjoint family the additivity of P(X in . | G) holds only off a null set depending on the family, and with enough such families the exceptional sets pile up. The route records only the bare non-existence claim (w02b-p15-008 lines 235-239); the attribution, references and explanation are absent. (2) Durrett's Theorem 4.1.17 (p. 215) assumes (S,S) nice, restated in its proof as a 1-1 map phi: S -> R with phi and phi^{-1} measurable; the handbook assumes a measurable isomorphism onto a Borel set E and calls this 'the source's standard Borel case' (lines 108-109) without stating the source's hypothesis or the relation between the two (the source's proof uses phi(A) in R, which requires a Borel image).

components.gap: Durrett presents the sphere example as Example 4.1.8, 'Borel's paradox' (p. 210, PDF p. 218): at first sight both the longitude and the angle along the great circle should be uniform; the longitude is uniform but the angle is not; the paradox disappears because in either formulation the angle is independent of the longitude, so its conditional law is the nonuniform unconditional one (more area near the equator than near the pole). The handbook proves the densities, independence and the nonuniform conditional law, but neither names Borel's paradox nor states the naive uniformity expectation that the example resolves; neither appears on the route for this example.
